newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian leaders try to breathe new life into budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian leaders try to breathe new life into budget.

text.p: Indian political leaders agreed on Friday to hold a special session of parliament later this month to try to salvage the nation's pathbreaking budget, which has been held hostage by a political crisis.

Representatives of all political parties met the speaker of the lower house, P.A. Sangma, who on Thursday had predicted a constitutional crisis if the investor-friendly budget fell victim to political turmoil.
"The nation is looking at us," a member of parliament who attended the meeting told Reuters. "Members of parliament should rise above party levels."
Another participant said: "There was general consensus that the budget should be passed."

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram earlier said efforts were under way to rescue the fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) budget. Parliament officials said the special session was tentatively set for April 21-23, but President Shankar Dayal Sharma would have to approve the dates.

"I am still hopeful that all political parties will find some way in which parliament can discharge its responsibility of passing the Finance Bill," Chidambaram told reporters during a break in parliamentary debate over a motion of confidence in Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Deve Gowda was expected to lose the vote of confidence, set for later on Friday, but his United Front coalition was holding talks to find a new leader and avert mid-term elections.
"As parliamentarians, it is possible to get together to pass the Finance Bill irrespective of the difficulties which the executive faces," Chidambaram said.
Presented by Chidambaram on February 28, the budget would slash corporate and personal income taxes, and reduce import tariffs.

"The budget for 1997/98 will be intact, and you can rest assured that even if the House is to be dissolved, it will not be so without passing the budget," the Press Trust of India quoted Congress leader Shivraj Patil as saying.
Share prices, which rallied after the budget was unveiled and fell back when it appeared under threat, were boosted by renewed expectations the budget plan might clear parliament.
The Bombay stock index ended 39.26 points, or 1.09 percent, higher at a provisional close of 3,637.

Despite widespread agreement that parliament should take up the budget regardless of the outcome of the political crisis, there was no guarantee it would emerge unscathed. Congress party leader Priya Ranjan Das Munshi, in his reply to the confidence motion, said: "The budget can wait."

Industry leaders said if the budget was not approved by parliament and the country headed for fresh elections, the economy would lose momentum, and investment plans and the flow of foreign funds would be put on hold.
"If there are elections, it would be a great setback to foreign investors," Tushar Sarda, president and chief executive officer of Daewoo Securities, told Reuters.
"The budget was appreciated by all sections of the society," Deve Gowda said, after moving the confidence motion.
Last month, parliament temporarily extended government spending programmes pending passage of the budget.
But some key provisions of the budget would lapse if it was not approved by May 14.
